article.title: The presidential election isn't a toss-up
article.subtitle: As our model launches, either Biden or Trump could easily win — but the odds are in the ex-president’s favor.

extraction.summary: Launch article for the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, which Silver describes as about 98% the same as his 2008-2020 FiveThirtyEight model, run in its 'polls-plus' form. At launch the model gives Trump about a 66% chance of winning the Electoral College, against 34% for Biden. Silver attributes this mainly to Biden's Electoral College disadvantage: he needs all three Rust Belt states, and uniform swing from 2020 implies he trails there. The economy-plus-incumbency fundamentals favor Biden only modestly and make up about 30% of the forecast, fading to zero by Election Day. The article also describes the nine-variable uncertainty index, which currently reads low, and polling-error calibration back to 1936. It closes with design-philosophy remarks on researcher degrees of freedom, overfitting, correlation errors in 2016 models, and resisting incentives to call races toss-ups. The full text is present despite the paywall flag.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model's methodology is about 98 percent the same as the 2020 FiveThirtyEight model. In everything but name it is the same model Silver ran at FiveThirtyEight from 2008 through 2020, and he retained the IP when he left Disney.
findings.evidence_quote: the methodology is about 98 percent the same as 2020, so the post only details the handful of changes

findings.statement: The published Silver Bulletin model is the 'polls-plus' version, which combines polls with incumbency and economic fundamentals. The polls-only version and the 'nowcast' were phased out in 2020.
findings.evidence_quote: the version of the model that we’re publishing at Silver Bulletin is what we used to call “polls-plus” at FiveThirtyEight

findings.statement: In the 2024 Silver Bulletin model, fundamentals made up about 30 percent of the forecast in late June 2024 and polls about 70 percent. The fundamentals weight gradually fades to zero by Election Day.
findings.rationale: Fundamentals models are prone to overfitting given small samples.
findings.evidence_quote: the fundamentals currently account for about 30 percent of the forecast, as compared to 70 percent for the polls, and this will gradually fade to zero by Election Day

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin presidential model, 'fundamentals' means only the economy and incumbency.
findings.evidence_quote: the fundamentals part of our model — which in the case of the Silver Bulletin, just means the economy and incumbency

findings.statement: Silver cautions against putting much weight on macro fundamentals. They have many possible specifications and few relevant elections, so they often overfit and replicate poorly out of sample. Fancy statistical techniques meant to prevent overfitting can actually make it worse.
findings.rationale: Small sample size of elections and many researcher degrees of freedom.
findings.evidence_quote: data scientists often talk themselves into thinking they’re avoiding overfitting by using some fancy statistical techniques when they’re actually making it worse

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin economic index uses six indicators, each expressed as a z-score from the incumbent party's standpoint (higher is better for the incumbent), and averages them. The indicators are real disposable personal income, the consumer price index, nonfarm payrolls, industrial production, personal consumption expenditures and the S&P 500.
findings.evidence_quote: These z-scores are evaluated from the standpoint of the incumbent party — higher is better for Biden

findings.statement: Economic index z-scores at June 26, 2024 launch, with projections for Nov. 5. The six-indicator average is projected at +0.04.

The economic index does not use actual GDP because it is updated only quarterly. It does use forecasted GDP from the Survey of Professional Forecasters to help project the other indicators forward to Election Day.
findings.evidence_quote: It does use forecasted GDP from the Survey of Professional Forecasters to help predict changes in the other indicators.

findings.statement: Real disposable (take-home) income growth is historically among the best economic variables at predicting election outcomes.
findings.evidence_quote: real take-home incomes, historically among the best economic variables at predicting election outcomes

findings.statement: By June 2024, the 2021-2023 high-inflation period was far enough in the past that it did not really hurt Biden in the model. This implies the economic index measures recent changes or a lookback window rather than cumulative price levels.
findings.evidence_quote: the period of very high inflation is enough in the rearview mirror to not really hurt Biden in the model

findings.statement: The 2024 model uses a slightly more complicated incumbency formula than before. It accounts for greater persistence in repeat matchups (same two candidates as last time) and for the incumbent party's vote share in the previous election. It distinguishes elected from appointed incumbents such as Ford.

quantities.name: Biden projected two-party vote, revised formula
Biden projected two-party vote, original formula

findings.rationale: Double-checked assumptions for the repeat matchup; the change makes essentially no difference.
findings.evidence_quote: accounts for greater persistence in repeat matchups like this one, and also for the incumbent party’s vote share in the previous election

findings.statement: The fundamentals model is calibrated on presidential elections dating back to 1880.
findings.rationale: Including high-polarization eras shows the incumbency advantage is negligible in such times.
findings.evidence_quote: The model is actually calibrated based on elections dating back to 1880.

findings.statement: Incumbency advantage is negligible in highly polarized eras, such as today or the late 19th and early 20th century (e.g., Grover Cleveland's close races). The large post-WWII incumbent margins, such as Reagan's 18-point re-election, are an artifact of an unusually low-polarization era.
findings.evidence_quote: In times of high polarization, like today, or in the early 20th century ... the incumbency advantage has been negligible.

findings.statement: The model does not consider the poor performance of incumbents in other countries, though Silver views it as external validation that incumbency is a minor advantage in the 2024 environment.
findings.evidence_quote: although the model doesn’t consider the poor performance of incumbents elsewhere around the world

findings.statement: In June 2024 the fundamentals projected Biden to win the national popular vote by 2 to 3 points (about 2.5). Because of his Electoral College disadvantage, that margin alone would make the race roughly a toss-up.
findings.evidence_quote: they currently project him to win the popular vote by 2 to 3 percentage points

findings.statement: The 2024 model removed the prior that Republicans do better in likely-voter polls than in registered-voter polls. This materially helps Biden, and Silver considers the evidence for the change highly robust.
findings.rationale: Evidence that the LV Republican advantage no longer holds is highly robust.
findings.evidence_quote: getting rid of the prior that Republicans tend to better in polls of likely voters rather than registered voters

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages adjust for likely versus registered voter populations; in 2024 this helps Biden.
findings.evidence_quote: making adjustments for factors like likely versus registered voters (this helps Biden)

findings.statement: The polling averages adjust for whether RFK Jr. is included in a poll. This adjustment has little effect on the Biden-Trump margin, somewhat contrary to conventional wisdom.
findings.evidence_quote: the presence or absence of RFK Jr. in polls (this doesn’t have much effect, somewhat contrary to the conventional wisdom)

findings.statement: The polling averages draw inferences from state polls to national polls and vice versa (a trend-line adjustment), which makes them more stable.
findings.evidence_quote: they make inferences from state polls to national polls and vice versa, which tend to make them more stable

findings.statement: The polling average weights each poll by its quality (pollster rating), sample size and recency.
The 2024 polling averages were backfilled to late February 2024.
findings.evidence_quote: We’ve backfilled the polling averages to late February.

findings.statement: The state polling-average table shows only contests surveyed by at least three distinct pollsters or with at least five polls. 'Week change' compares with the average seven days earlier, and 'month change' compares with thirty days earlier.

Polling averages on June 26, 2024 (Biden / Trump / Kennedy): National 41.3/42.3/8.0; PA 43.2/44.6/5.4; MI 42.1/43.2/6.2; WI 42.7/43.2/6.9; GA 39.2/44.7/6.5; AZ 38.7/43.9/8.0; NC 38.4/45.1/7.0; NV 39.3/44.1/7.7; FL 37.9/45.9/6.1; TX 36.8/46.1/7.4. Nationally, Biden gained 1 point over the month but lost 0.4 over the week.

The model blends each state's polling average with a series of regression-based estimates that infer what the state's polling 'should' be from polls in other states and national numbers. The historically most reliable of these is uniform swing from the previous election.
findings.rationale: Uniform swing has historically been the most reliable of these techniques.
findings.evidence_quote: the one that has historically been most reliable is indeed to assume some sort of uniform swing from the previous election

findings.statement: The regression estimate gets less weight in heavily polled states such as Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania. Weight on the regression is inversely related to the amount of state polling.
findings.evidence_quote: Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania are fairly robustly polled — so the regression estimate doesn’t get that much weight

findings.statement: Some 2016 models gave Clinton as little as a 1 percent chance of losing. Silver calls them wrong, not just unlucky, because they treated similar states such as Michigan and Wisconsin as relatively uncorrelated, an assumption that can be validated empirically as false.

quantities.name: Clinton loss probability in some 2016 models

findings.rationale: Similar states move in similar directions from election to election.
findings.evidence_quote: They were wrong because they made obviously wrong assumptions, especially that the outcomes in similar states such as Michigan and Wisconsin were relatively uncorrelated.

findings.statement: In the Silver Bulletin model, Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania are heavily but not perfectly correlated. Demographic differences matter: Wisconsin is more rural, and Michigan has the largest Arab/Muslim/Palestinian population. In simulations, Biden wins at least one of the three 54% of the time but all three only 32% of the time.

quantities.name: P(Biden wins at least one of MI/WI/PA)

findings.rationale: Winning several correlated bets is still hard (same-game parlay analogy).
findings.evidence_quote: In our simulations, Biden wins at least one of these states 54 percent of the time. But he wins all three of them in only 32 percent of simulations.

findings.statement: Conditional on winning Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania, Biden wins the Electoral College about 97% of the time in simulations. The remaining risk comes from states such as NH, VA, NM, MN and NE-2.

quantities.name: P(Biden EC win | wins MI, WI, PA)

findings.evidence_quote: conditional on winning Wisconsin and Michigan and Pennsylvania, Biden wins the Electoral College about 97 percent of the time

findings.statement: Biden winning exactly 270 electoral votes (Trump 268) is among the modal outcomes of the model's electoral vote distribution, yet occurs only 3-4% of the time.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s still only a 3 to 4 percent chance of it occurring, according to the forecast

findings.statement: The 2024 model runs 40,000 simulations. Launch outputs: Biden 33.7% EC, 51.0% popular vote, 250.4 expected EV, 47.2% vote share. Trump 65.7% EC, 49.0% popular vote, 287.2 EV, 47.1% vote share. Kennedy 0.0% EC, 0.4 EV, 4.3% vote share. No majority 0.5%.

Model simulations allow RFK Jr. to win some electoral votes, which can produce no-majority outcomes alongside 269-269 ties. The model considers it very, very unlikely he carries the Electoral College.
findings.evidence_quote: The model does contemplate the possibility that Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. could win some electoral votes

findings.statement: No-majority outcomes are reported separately rather than assigned to a candidate. Silver notes they would probably resolve to Trump through a House contingent election under the 12th Amendment, given the likely Republican advantage in state congressional delegations.
findings.evidence_quote: those cases will probably resolve to Trump because of the likely Republican advantage in congressional delegations in the U.S. House under the 12th Amendment

findings.statement: At launch the model assumes the major-party nominees are Biden and Trump and that nobody drops out. Forecasts are therefore conditional predictions that ignore the actuarial chance of candidate replacement.
findings.evidence_quote: I’ll make the same assumption made by the model: that the major-party candidates will be Joe Biden and Donald Trump

findings.statement: The uncertainty index estimates overall error in the system. It has a modest effect on expected Election Day polling error and a much bigger effect on expected poll volatility (drift) between now and the election.
findings.evidence_quote: The uncertainty index has a modest effect on how much error the model expects there to be in the polls on Election Day — but the much bigger effect is on how much volatility

findings.statement: The 2024 uncertainty index uses nine variables, up from eight in 2020. The new variable captures whether candidates are repeat candidates: when both were on the last ballot, they are better known and the polls are less volatile.
findings.rationale: Repeat candidates are better known by voters.
findings.evidence_quote: repeat candidates tend to produce less volatility in the polls than first-time ones since they are better known by voters. (This is the factor we newly account for this year.)

findings.statement: The nine uncertainty index variables are: (1) poll stability to date; (2) polarization level; (3) repeat candidates; (4) economic volatility; (5) polling volume; (6) the gap between polls and fundamentals; (7) the volume of news, measured by the number of full-width New York Times headlines; (8) the undecided vote share; (9) third-party vote share. Higher stability, polarization, polling volume and repeat candidates mean lower uncertainty. Higher undecided and third-party shares mean higher uncertainty.
findings.evidence_quote: as measured by the number of full-width New York Times headlines

findings.statement: In June 2024, seven of the nine uncertainty index factors pointed toward low uncertainty and two (high undecided vote, Kennedy's third-party share) toward higher. The index read 'low' rather than the 'average' Silver expected.
findings.evidence_quote: So by a 7-2 verdict, the factors in the uncertainty index imply that this will be a relatively stable race.

findings.statement: When calculating future uncertainty, the model treats each scheduled presidential debate as essentially adding time to the clock. With two debates scheduled instead of three in 2024, expected uncertainty is slightly lower.
findings.evidence_quote: it considers presidential debates to essentially put more time on the clock in calculating future uncertainty

findings.statement: The model calibrates Election Day polling accuracy on elections back to 1936, including big misses like 1948. This makes expected polling error about 35 percent higher than training only on recent polling, so the model anticipates possible secular decline from the 'Golden Age of Polling' of roughly 2004-2012.

quantities.name: expected error inflation vs recent-only training

findings.rationale: Conservative assumptions about systematic polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: This makes the error it expects about 35 percent higher than if we’d trained it only on more recent polling.

findings.statement: The direction of polling error is hard to predict, so the model treats a candidate as roughly as likely to underperform their polls as to overperform them. The error is unbiased in direction.
findings.evidence_quote: it’s hard to predict the direction of polling error. Biden could easily overachieve his current polls — but it’s roughly as likely that he’ll underachieve them instead

findings.statement: Running the 2020 model unchanged, apart from removing COVID-related components, would give largely similar results with Biden a slightly heavier underdog. The 2024 changes on net slightly help Biden.
findings.evidence_quote: if I’d just run the 2020 version of the model back without changing anything at all (other than removing COVID-related stuff), the results would be largely similar but Biden would be a slightly heavier underdog

findings.statement: The 2020 model contained COVID-related components that were removed for 2024.
findings.evidence_quote: other than removing COVID-related stuff

findings.statement: A model should sometimes surprise its builder. Always matching intuition suggests wasted effort or reverse-engineering assumptions to match priors. Extremely counterintuitive outputs, such as Obama at 96% in June 2012, still warrant checking for bugs or flaws, so domain knowledge plays a role.
findings.rationale: Avoid tuning to priors while catching bugs.
findings.evidence_quote: I’d essentially worked backward, tweaking the assumptions in the model until they matched my priors

findings.statement: Presidential forecasting has tiny samples: 2024 is only the 20th presidential election since WWII and roughly the 10th-12th with robust state-level polling. As a result there is no single right model. Congressional forecasting, with almost 500 relatively independent races per cycle, allows assumptions to be tested better.
findings.evidence_quote: This is only the 20th presidential election since World War II, and only roughly the 10th or 12th with any sort of robust, state-by-state polling data.

findings.statement: House and Senate races are correlated with each other, but less than presidential state outcomes, because each contest has different candidates. There can be considerable regional variation, as in 2022.
findings.evidence_quote: House and Senate races are correlated with one another — just not to the same degree that the presidential race is

findings.statement: In June 2024, other models showed Trump between 50% (538's new model) and 71% (The Economist). Silver disagrees with them but considers none unreasonable. He notes that only his model has a long out-of-sample track record, now 16 years.
findings.evidence_quote: which show Trump with anything from a 50 percent chance (538’s new model) to a 71 percent chance (the Economist) of winning

findings.statement: Even a polling average involves many researcher degrees of freedom: which polls to include, how to weight them, how much to prioritize recency. Fundamentals add essentially infinite further choices.
findings.evidence_quote: there are basically infinite “researcher degrees of freedom” in exactly how you do it

findings.statement: Forecasters and pundits are incentivized to call races toss-ups to avoid blame. A 65/35 forecast will still be wrong about a third of the time, and calling such a race a toss-up is a 'white lie' that shirks accountability.
findings.evidence_quote: At 65/35, you’re being more definitive — so you’ll get blamed more for an incorrect forecast — but you’re still going to be wrong a lot: about a third of the time.

findings.statement: Silver states that his personal view matches the model's 66% Trump forecast and that he will disclose any divergence. Sometimes models have known flaws not yet fixed; he cites the RAPTOR NBA model having too much home-court advantage.
findings.evidence_quote: If we reach a point where my mental model and the Silver Bulletin model diverge, I’ll tell you that. But right now they don’t diverge at all.

findings.statement: Product details: the polling averages are free, while the forecast probabilities are paywalled. Narrative updates run about weekly through Labor Day and more frequently after. Landing-page updates are planned a few times a week after backend automation.
findings.evidence_quote: the polling averages will be available for everyone — but the forecast and probabilistic components of the model are for paid subscribers

findings.statement: Poll stability to date predicts future stability. Highly stable races such as 2012 feature many 'fake turning points' that don't move the race. Volatile years such as 2016 and the uncertain 2020 warranted higher model uncertainty.
findings.evidence_quote: The polls have been extremely stable so far, which tends to predict future stability.

political_insights.insight: In 2020 Michigan was 2.7, Pennsylvania 3.3 and Wisconsin 3.8 points right of the national margin. Under uniform swing, a tied national race implies Trump leads the Rust Belt, so a tied national polling average is not a toss-up. 2024 resembles 2012 in reverse.
political_insights.evidence: 2020 state-vs-national margins; Biden running about 5 points worse than his 4.5-point 2020 margin
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model the state-national gap from the prior election rather than treating national polls as decisive.

political_insights.insight: In highly polarized eras, elections tend toward 50/50 and incumbency advantage is negligible.
political_insights.evidence: Cleveland-era close races; post-WWII landslides as low-polarization artifacts
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Shrink incumbency effects and fundamentals-based margins in polarized eras.

political_insights.insight: Biden's age, cumulative price increases from 2021-23 inflation, a global anti-incumbent mood, and the lowest approval of any re-election candidate since Bush 41 or Carter make his losses overdetermined.
political_insights.evidence: About 1 in 70 Biden-leaning voters defecting over age would close the gap between the fundamentals (Biden +2.5) and the polls (Biden -0.5).
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Fundamentals indices may miss candidate-specific factors.

political_insights.insight: Trump substantially outperformed his polls in 2016 and 2020. Democrats outperforming polls in 2022 is 'sort of a myth', though they beat conventional wisdom.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Do not assume the direction of polling error.

political_insights.insight: Trump's hush-money conviction probably helped Biden slightly at the margin but did not shake up the race; Biden trended up about 1 point over the month.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Scandal events may produce only marginal shifts.

political_insights.insight: Biden trailed by mid-single digits in high-quality polls of Georgia, Arizona and Nevada; the model gave him a 22% chance in Arizona. He has no backup path if any Rust Belt state falls.
Only two debates were scheduled, versus the usual three, and the first was on June 27, 2024, an opportunity for Biden to change the race.

open_questions: Exact functional form of the decay of the fundamentals weight from 30% to 0 by Election Day.
Weights and functional form of the six indicators in the economic index and how z-scores map to vote share.
Exact revised incumbency formula: the repeat-matchup persistence term and the previous incumbent-party vote share term.
How the nine uncertainty index variables are combined and scaled into error/drift standard deviations.
Specification of the regression-based state estimates and the blend weights versus polling volume.
Form of the correlation structure between states (demographic similarity and regional factors).
How much time-on-the-clock each debate adds in the uncertainty calculation.
Distribution used for polling error (fat tails?) and its magnitude after the 1936-based calibration.
Specifics of the likely-voter/registered-voter adjustment now that the Republican LV prior is removed.
How the RFK Jr. inclusion adjustment is computed.
How undecided and third-party votes are allocated in simulations.
